display.text: A variable whose values place each observation in one of several mutually exclusive categories. Numerical category codes do not give the categories arithmetic meaning. Also called qualitative variable.
A random variable that can take any value within an interval, commonly obtained by measurement. Rounding recorded measurements does not change the underlying continuous quantity.
A random variable with a finite or countably infinite list of distinct possible values, commonly obtained by counting.
Organizing and summarizing collected data to reveal patterns and make the information understandable. Abbreviated EDA.
A person or object described by a dataset; an individual typically occupies one row of a data table. Also called case.
A number used as a category label, such as a hospital identifier; its numerical appearance does not make the variable quantitative.
The entire group of people, animals, objects, or other individuals about which a study seeks information.
A numerical description of how likely outcomes are, used in this unit to connect sample information with conclusions about a population.
A variable with numerical values representing counts or measurements for which arithmetic comparisons are meaningful.
A process, such as a coin toss or random selection, whose particular outcome is uncertain before it occurs. Also called trial.
A quantity whose value is determined by a random outcome. Formally, it assigns one numerical value to each outcome; the course also informally refers to randomly observed categorical variables.
The fraction of observations in which a specified outcome occurs; in an observational setting it is used to estimate the outcome's probability.
A sample that reflects the population's relevant characteristics well enough to support the intended conclusions about it.
A subgroup of a population from which data are collected to learn about that population.
The set of all possible outcomes of a random experiment; it may be a list of outcomes or a continuous interval. Notation: S.
Using a chance process or computer-generated random values to imitate outcomes of a specified situation or model.
Drawing conclusions about a population from sample data while accounting for uncertainty through probability.
The process of collecting, summarizing, and interpreting data to obtain useful information.
A probability obtained from a specified chance model and probability principles, rather than estimated from observed frequencies.
A characteristic of an individual that can take different values across individuals or observations.
